questions.q: Per this lesson, why isn't an untested DR plan a real plan?
options: SQL Server automatically invalidates any plan that hasn't been tested
Testing is only necessary for Availability Groups, not other DR technologies
An untested plan is fine as long as it's reviewed by a manager
A written plan encodes assumptions that can silently go stale, and the only way to know it still works is to actually exercise it
questions.explain: Assumptions like backup locations, role assignments, and configuration details can drift over time without anyone noticing until the plan is exercised.

questions.q: What does a tabletop exercise validate, and what can't it validate, per this lesson?
options: It only tests network latency between sites
It validates the technical steps exactly like a real failover drill would
It has no value and should be skipped in favor of real drills only
It validates the plan's logic, roles, and escalation points, but not whether the actual technical steps (like a restore command) still work
questions.explain: A tabletop is a talk-through without touching real systems — good for surfacing plan gaps, but it can't confirm the technical steps actually execute correctly.

questions.q: What does a real failover drill validate that a tabletop exercise cannot?
options: Whether the people involved know their names and titles
Only whether the backup files exist on disk
Nothing — a failover drill provides no additional value over a tabletop
Whether the runbook's actual commands work against the current environment and whether the real RTO is met
questions.explain: A real drill actually executes recovery steps, which is the only way to confirm the technical procedure and timing actually hold up.

questions.q: What separates a good runbook step from a vague one, per this lesson?
options: Actual commands, exact paths/servers/access, and verification steps — not phrases like 'restore the database' or 'the usual backup location'
Runbooks should never include actual T-SQL commands, only descriptions
A good runbook step should always be phrased as generally as possible so it applies to any system
Verification steps are optional and add unnecessary length
questions.explain: A good runbook is specific enough that someone unfamiliar with the original system could follow it under pressure, including confirming the recovery actually worked.

questions.q: A team runs tabletop exercises quarterly but has never done a real AG failover. What real risk remains, per this lesson?
options: The team's roles and responsibilities are guaranteed to be wrong
Whether the actual failover technically works and meets the RTO has never been confirmed — only the plan's logic has been validated
There is no remaining risk since tabletop exercises are equivalent to real drills
Tabletop exercises make real failover drills unnecessary forever
questions.explain: Tabletop exercises validate plan logic, not technical execution — without a real drill, it's unknown whether the failover actually works as documented.
